reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents with sudden severe unilateral eye pain, marked blurring, and haloes around lights, often with nausea, vomiting, and headache that can mimic a systemic illness
The affected eye is red with circumcorneal (ciliary) injection, a hazy oedematous cornea, and a fixed mid-dilated oval pupil
Intraocular pressure is markedly elevated, frequently well above 40 mmHg, and the globe feels stony hard to gentle palpation
Typically affects hypermetropic (long-sighted) eyes with shallow anterior chambers, and is often precipitated in dim light, by stress, or by pupil-dilating drugs
Immediate goal is to lower intraocular pressure with combined topical and systemic pressure-lowering therapy plus a topical miotic to break the attack
Definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy once the cornea clears, and the fellow eye should receive prophylactic iridotomy because it is anatomically at risk
Gonioscopy of both eyes confirms a closed or occludable angle and distinguishes it from open-angle mechanisms
reference.pathophysiology: In predisposed eyes with a shallow anterior chamber and short axial length, the peripheral iris crowds the drainage angle. When the pupil becomes mid-dilated, relative pupillary block impedes aqueous flow from the posterior to the anterior chamber, so pressure builds behind the iris and bows it forward against the trabecular meshwork. This apposition abruptly obstructs aqueous outflow, causing a rapid and severe rise in intraocular pressure that compromises the optic nerve head and corneal endothelium if not relieved promptly.
additionalDifferentials: Cluster headache or migraine (for the pain component)
additionalInvestigations: Applanation or non-contact tonometry to quantify the raised intraocular pressure
Slit-lamp examination to assess corneal oedema, chamber depth, and pupil reaction
Gonioscopy of both eyes to demonstrate the occludable/closed angle
Optic disc assessment for glaucomatous cupping once the media clear
Anterior segment OCT or ultrasound biomicroscopy to document angle configuration
redFlags: Sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency — irreversible optic nerve damage can occur within hours of sustained high pressure
Stony-hard eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil and corneal haze requires immediate ophthalmology referral
Systemic nausea and vomiting can mask the ocular origin and delay treatment
Failure of the fellow eye to receive prophylactic iridotomy risks a subsequent contralateral attack
reference.prognosis: Prompt reduction of pressure and timely iridotomy usually preserve vision, but delayed treatment can cause permanent optic nerve damage and irreversible loss of sight.
pitfalls: Mistaking the vomiting and headache for a gastrointestinal or neurological illness and missing the ocular cause
Pharmacologically dilating a shallow-chambered eye and precipitating an attack
Forgetting prophylactic treatment of the anatomically predisposed fellow eye
Assuming a normal pressure once the acute attack settles without confirming the angle is open
management: Immediate intraocular pressure lowering with combined topical agents (a beta-blocker, alpha-agonist and prostaglandin analogue) plus systemic acetazolamide, adding an intravenous hyperosmotic such as mannitol if needed
Topical pilocarpine as a miotic to constrict the pupil and break the pupillary block once pressure begins to fall
Topical corticosteroids to reduce the associated intraocular inflammation
Analgesia and antiemetics for the pain and vomiting that accompany the attack
Definitive laser peripheral iridotomy once the cornea clears, with lens extraction as an alternative definitive option
Prophylactic laser peripheral iridotomy to the anatomically at-risk fellow eye
Urgent ophthalmology referral, with ongoing intraocular pressure and optic disc monitoring
